newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-EMI faces 50 mln pound currency hit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMI faces 50 mln pound currency hit.

text.p: British music company EMI Group Plc said on Friday that the strong pound was likely to dent profits this year by as much as 50 million pounds ($84 million).
Chairman Sir Colin Southgate told the company's annual meeting that growth remained sluggish in many of the world's major music markets but the key U.S. sector was showing signs of improvement.
"The short-term economic climate for EMI remains challenging but there are signs of recovery in the U.S. market," he said.

EMI's market share in the United States has increased to almost 13 percent in recent weeks after sliding to 10 percent. The rise has been driven by sales of The Spice Girls debut album "Spice", which has been in the top five in the U.S. for four months.
EMI shares, which have performed poorly since the company demerged from rentals group Thorn last August, initially slipped further on the news but later recovered to trade unchanged at 1083.5 pence.
They have fallen steadily from a post-demerger high of 1460p on worries over the state of the $40 billion global music market and as takeover speculation receded.

Share analysts noted that the predicted 45-50 million pound impact from sterling compared with an earlier forecast of a 30 million pound hit for EMI, which generates 80 percent of its revenues abroad.
They also said that interest charges would rise as the result of a plan approved at the meeting to return 500 million pounds to shareholders. The buyback will be funded through borrowing.
Brokerage Dresdner Kleinwort Benson this week downgraded its profit forecast to 388 million pounds, only just ahead of last year's 380.5 million. Others say profits could dip below that level.
EMI is one of the five music majors which dominate the business around the globe. Its main rivals are PolyGram NV, Sony, Bertelsmann and Warner Bros.
EMI took a 117 million pound charge last year as it restructures its operations in the U.S. in a bid to end its long-standing weakness there.
"Currently we are number-three in the world. To be number-one we will have to crack the U.S. market and that is exactly what our restructuring plans are intended to achieve," said Southgate.
A layer of management has been removed and the New York office of the EMI Capitol label closed.
The moves are designed ultimately to cut costs by an annual 35-40 million pounds.

Southgate said EMI, celebrating its centenary in 1997, had a strong release schedule including material from Janet Jackson, the Rolling Stones and a second Spice Girls album, which should be out before Christmas.($= 0.598 British Pounds)
